strengths: The paper presents an intuitive idea: learn a low-dimensional collective variable as the conditioning bottleneck of a time-lagged generative model, supplemented by an autocorrelation objective.
The evaluation uses downstream enhanced-sampling simulations rather than relying only on latent-space visualizations, and compares against relevant supervised and time-lagged baselines.
Under the reported SMD protocol, TLC obtains a substantially better energy–success tradeoff than the baselines, while its OPES free-energy estimate is within the stated tolerance of the reference.
The paper includes useful sensitivity visualizations and ablations of the autocorrelation loss and input representation.
weaknesses: The evidence is limited to alanine dipeptide, a small canonical benchmark with known dihedral collective variables. One system and one transition direction are insufficient to establish generality, scalability, or significance for realistic molecular systems.

The novelty over time-lagged autoencoders and VDE is modest, and the paper provides neither a theoretical argument nor a controlled ablation showing that flow matching—rather than the autocorrelation loss, aligned-coordinate representation, or model capacity—causes the improvement. Generation quality and whether the generator actually uses the learned condition are never evaluated.

The central flow-matching formulation is underspecified and apparently inconsistent: Equation 7 feeds x_t and t to the vector field while omitting the interpolated noisy sample x_r, flow time r, Gaussian source x_0, and explicit target x_{t+tau}-x_0 required by the preceding construction. The manuscript also incorrectly describes the finite-lag transition distribution as a conditional Boltzmann distribution.

The SMD comparison is heavily confounded. A different force constant is selected for every method, learned CVs can have very different gradients despite range normalization, selection uses an arbitrary 1000 kJ/mol cutoff, and transition energy is averaged only over successful trajectories. Pareto curves across force constants, matched effective bias strength, model-training seeds, and statistical comparisons are absent. The stated 0.5-degree hit threshold also appears inconsistent with the plotted target region and needs verification.

The OPES experiment does not demonstrate a clear advantage: several baselines have more accurate and much lower-variance free-energy estimates than TLC. Method-specific SIGMA values are used without a tuning protocol, only one trajectory is visualized, and transition counts, effective sample sizes, and convergence-time comparisons are missing.

The representation comparison is not adequately controlled. The distance-based TLC ablation degrades dramatically, while baseline methods use differing representations. Moreover, all CVs are normalized using a separate 100 ns metadynamics trajectory containing transition-region samples, weakening the claim that the pipeline uses no transition data and reducing practical applicability.

Reproducibility is poor: the code link is broken, and key details such as lambda, optimizer, epochs, batch size, number of training samples, complete EGNN/generator architecture, flow noise settings, and hyperparameter-selection procedures are absent. VDE is also omitted from the architecture table, and results are not reported across independently trained models.

strengths: The paper addresses an important ML-for-science problem: learning differentiable collective variables for rare-event molecular sampling.
Using a low-dimensional condition for time-lagged flow matching is intuitive and potentially more expressive than point-reconstruction autoencoders; the autocorrelation term is also well motivated.
The evaluation applies learned CVs in actual SMD and OPES simulations, compares against five learned-CV baselines, and includes useful qualitative analyses and component ablations.
On alanine dipeptide, TLC obtains an interesting reported SMD result—60.93% target hits with substantially lower transition energy—and its OPES free-energy estimate is close to the reference.
weaknesses: The evidence is too narrow for a top-tier claim: every experiment uses the same small, well-understood alanine-dipeptide system. There is no larger or qualitatively different molecule, scalability analysis, lag-time study, latent-dimension study, or evaluation across training seeds.

The central mathematical specification is incomplete or inconsistent. Equation 7 overloads physical time with flow time, evaluates the vector field at the molecular frame rather than a sampled flow interpolant, and omits the Gaussian-source/interpolation expectation required by Equations 4–6. Moreover, a time-lagged transition distribution is repeatedly called a conditional Boltzmann distribution without justification. Consequently, the method is not precisely reproducible from the paper, nor is it established that its objective specifically identifies slow modes.

The principal comparison is confounded by input representation. TLC uses aligned Cartesian coordinates, whereas DeepLDA, DeepTDA, and DeepTICA use pairwise distances; the authors' own ablation changes SMD target-hit rate from 60.93% to 7.81% when TLC uses distances. A controlled comparison isolating the generative objective from representation and autocorrelation choices is therefore essential. The generative model's conditional sample quality is never evaluated either.

The SMD protocol contains major inconsistencies. Force constants are selected separately using performance-related criteria, yet no validation split is described; the appendix states a search range of 100–1000 while Table 1 reports 1200 for TAE. The transition-energy quantity is insufficiently defined, has dramatically different scales across methods, and is averaged only over successful paths. The stated 0.5-degree hit threshold also appears inconsistent with the plotted target region. These issues undermine the headline improvement.

The OPES results do not demonstrate superiority: nearly every method lies within the stated accuracy tolerance, TLC has greater uncertainty than several baselines, only four trajectories are used, and method-specific SIGMA values are not justified through a common tuning protocol or sensitivity analysis.

The claim of learning without transition data is overstated because a 100 ns oracle metadynamics trajectory generated with the known dihedral CVs—including transition-region configurations—is used to normalize learned CVs for downstream simulations. Training trajectories can also contain transition configurations even though cross-sign lagged pairs are removed.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the code statement is incomplete, VDE is missing from the architecture table, and key details such as the flow/EGNN architecture, autocorrelation weight, interpolation noise, optimizer, batch size, training duration, model-selection procedure, and deployment of differentiable Kabsch alignment in bias-force calculations are absent. Several relevant modern CV-learning baselines are also omitted.

Moreover, strongly forced SMD trajectories are not validated as physically representative transition paths.

The OPES evaluation is partly circular and coordinate-dependent. Each method is normalized, partitioned into folded/unfolded basins by bisecting its own CV range, and evaluated against a reference PMF projected onto that same CV using the full DESRES trajectory. Consequently, the purported physical reference free energies vary substantially—and sometimes change sign—across methods. Full-trajectory normalization and state calibration also leak reference information unavailable in a realistic deployment.

The quantitative evidence is weak and unstable. Only three or four runs are used, one run is removed post hoc as an outlier, uncertainty is often as large as or larger than the apparent improvements, and no confidence intervals or statistical tests are provided. BIOEMU-CV remains poorly converged on Trp-cage and especially BBA, and it is not consistently best on PMF error, VAMP score, or committor correlation.

The benefit of BioEmu pretraining is not isolated. There is no randomly initialized or comparably sized generative-backbone control, no audit of overlap between BioEmu pretraining data and these common miniproteins, and no comparison with a simpler future-prediction objective using the same encoder. Thus the experiments do not establish that a protein foundation model is responsible for the gains.

The claimed scalability and practical value are overstated. Separate models are trained using 50,000 frames sampled from complete 106–223 microsecond trajectories containing the relevant states, and evaluation covers only 10-, 20-, and 28-residue miniproteins. There is no held-out-protein generalization, independent-trajectory split, scarce-transition regime, or data-efficiency study.

The comparison set is incomplete for a claimed comprehensive benchmark. Simple TICA/PCA appear only in a limited appendix experiment, while RMSD-only, native-contact, other handcrafted CVs, and stronger recent dynamical representation methods are absent. Applying one architecture and optimization setup to very different baseline objectives also does not demonstrate that the baselines were adequately tuned.

The central assertion that the bottleneck necessarily captures slow dynamics is not theoretically justified or directly tested. The training lag and its units are not clearly specified, no lag-sensitivity study is given, and the conditional time-lagged generation quality is never evaluated.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the code-release sentence is unfinished, run-count and outlier-removal descriptions conflict, the stated [45,100,100,1] architecture is inconsistent with the 190- and 378-dimensional protein inputs, and several essential architecture and optimization details are missing. Overall, the idea is plausible and the simulation effort is notable, but major evaluation confounds leave the main claims insufficiently supported for acceptance.
